evals.prompt: A team wants to serve a 70B instruct model (bf16) on two A100 80GB GPUs in one node with a 32K context window. Draft the vllm serve command with serving flags, explain the memory and parallelism reasoning, and state what to verify after startup.
evals.expected_output: A pinned serving plan with model/revision, stable served name, tensor parallel size 2, a 32768 prompt-plus-output limit, and an explicit memory budget. Roughly 140 GB of bf16 weights makes two 80 GB GPUs a candidate, not proof that 32K requests at the desired overlap fit after runtime overhead. Distinguish the request admission limit from the profiled KV pool and actual resident lengths; do not promise a capacity doubling from halving the configured limit. Verify startup profiling/KV capacity, the served name, and a representative generated response. Record the pinned config as the rollback unit; no deployment is authorized by a request to draft it.
assertions: The command pins model, revision, served-model-name, tensor-parallel-size 2, max-model-len, and gpu-memory-utilization
Uses roughly 140 GB of bf16 weights to assess the two-GPU plan without guaranteeing the target workload fits
Distinguishes the max-model-len admission limit from the allocated KV pool and actual resident token demand
Verification includes startup memory profiling, /v1/models, and a representative chat request
The serving config template is used so the deployment is reproducible and rollback is a pinned-image redeploy

evals.prompt: Our 8B model in bf16 takes 16GB of VRAM and we want to serve 256 concurrent long-context requests. We have a single 80GB H100. Should we quantize, enable tensor parallelism, or both, and what trade-offs should we record before changing anything?
evals.expected_output: Measure a baseline before choosing memory changes: capture the allocated KV pool and startup estimate with its assumed length, then measure actual input/output distributions, queueing, preemption and latency at increasing request overlap. The requested 256 concurrency is not assumed safe. Tensor parallelism cannot shard across additional GPUs when only one H100 exists. Evaluate compatible weight and KV quantization separately with quality tests and matched runs. max-model-len is a request limit, max-num-seqs is an iteration limit, and neither establishes SLO capacity. Record and verify every proposed change rather than promising capacity from memory arithmetic.
assertions: Requires a measured baseline before claiming the requested concurrency is supportable
Tensor parallelism is correctly deemed not applicable on a single GPU
Quantization (FP8/INT4 weights) and kv-cache-dtype fp8 are evaluated as the memory levers, with quality trade-offs stated
Correlates KV occupancy with waiting requests and preemption before diagnosing capacity
Verification re-runs the frozen benchmark and a quality spot-check under matched conditions

evals.prompt: We started vllm serve with a chat model and the OpenAI SDK returns a 404 for /v1/chat/completions, while /v1/models works. Diagnose the likely causes and describe how to verify the fix, without exposing the server.
evals.expected_output: A diagnostic sequence over the read-only probes: confirm /health and /v1/models respond, then check what /v1/models actually lists and compare it with the model name the client sends, since a served-model-name mismatch or an unserved model id produces 404-style failures on inference routes. The next checks are version and load state, and the server log for whether the model loaded and which endpoints are registered on this release, because vLLM serves /v1/chat/completions only for text-generation models that carry a chat template; a model without a chat template cannot serve chat and needs --chat-template, and some pooling or embedding models do not register chat endpoints at all. The fix is verified by sending one bounded chat request with the exact served model name and checking for generated tokens, and by confirming the server is only reachable on the intended interface with API auth or a reverse proxy in place. The response does not expose logs or tokens and treats any bind-address or API-key change as a confirmed mutation.
assertions: Diagnosis starts with /health, /v1/models, and the served model name versus the client's model field
Chat templates and model type (generative versus pooling) are named as the cause of missing /v1/chat/completions routes
The fix is verified with one bounded chat request returning generated tokens
Exposure controls (bind address, API keys, reverse proxy) are checked without dumping logs or secrets
A bind or auth change is treated as a mutation requiring confirmation

evals.prompt: A colleague claims a vLLM upgrade doubled our token throughput: 420 tok/s before, 850 tok/s after. Review their evidence before we roll the upgrade to production.
evals.expected_output: Treat 420 versus 850 tok/s as an unproven comparison until matched benchmark records are available. Freeze model/revision, tokenizer/template, precision, hardware, parallelism, request limits, batching, workload lengths, rate/overlap, sampling and cache cohorts; engine version is the declared variable. Ask for raw per-request latency and failures, aggregate throughput, sample sizes and repeated-run variance. Check whether precision, cache warmth, length/truncation or concurrency changed, without assuming a real doubling is impossible. Separate aggregate throughput from per-request TTFT/TPOT and task outcomes. Use the run-record template; rollout requires the agreed SLO and acceptance evidence, not just the larger number.
assertions: The review demands matched conditions (version, model, quant, parallelism, context, batching, GPU, workload) on both sides
Raw vllm bench serve output with throughput, TTFT/TPOT/ITL percentiles, and variance is required, not a single number
A suspicious doubling is probed for a mismatch in concurrency, dataset, or precision
Throughput and latency (TTFT/TPOT under load) are treated as separate metrics
The benchmark run record template is required on both sides before the upgrade ships
Checks cache state and actual output lengths or truncation as possible comparison confounders

evals.prompt: Our vLLM server reports gpu_cache_usage_perc above 0.95 with requests waiting, and p50 latency is fine but p99 spiked. We already run with default batching settings. What should we change, and what should we measure?
evals.expected_output: Investigate pressure before tuning: cache occupancy and waiting warrant correlating preemption, request lengths, TTFT/TPOT tails, running/queued load and scheduler limits. Inspect resolved V1 settings because chunked prefill and prefix caching may already be enabled. Test one targeted change such as concurrency admission, a chunked-prefill token budget, reduced actual prompt/output demand or scale-out. Lowering max-model-len alone does not free KV for unchanged real lengths. Evaluate shared-prefix reuse with cold/warm controls and distinguish prefill savings from decoding. Re-run matched repeated benchmarks with per-request tails and task outcomes, keeping all mutations gated.
assertions: Correlates high KV occupancy and waiting with preemption or latency evidence before declaring the capacity bottleneck
Inspects resolved chunked-prefill and prefix-cache settings before recommending enablement
Proposes a bounded experiment using concurrency, a prefill token budget, actual token demand, or scale-out
Does not claim lowering max-model-len alone frees KV memory at unchanged actual token lengths
Evaluates prefix reuse with cache-state controls rather than promising faster decoding
Changes one variable at a time under matched benchmark conditions
Requires repeated per-request tail-latency evidence rather than one aggregate or median result

evals.prompt: We upgraded the vllm/vllm-openai image from :v0.25.1 to :v0.26.0 and the server now crashes at startup with a CUDA out of memory error, even though the model did not change. Diagnose and decide: fix forward or roll back?
evals.expected_output: A bounded diagnosis that starts with the read-only evidence: confirm the exact image digest on both versions, the serving args, the model revision, and the GPU inventory (nvidia-smi), then compare the startup logs of the failing v0.26.0 run against the v0.25.1 run. OOM at startup after an engine upgrade warrants checking the failing allocation phase, competing load, changed memory defaults and changed flag semantics: vLLM releases change default KV cache allocation, max-model-len derivation, CUDA graph capture, and flag names, so the same config may now reserve more memory; the fix-forward path re-reads the v0.26.0 release notes for changed defaults, tests a targeted memory-budget or execution-setting change on the scratch instance without assuming a smaller request limit shrinks the KV pool, validates the model loads and passes the frozen benchmark, and only then redeploys. The rollback path is already cheap because the previous pinned image and serving config were recorded: redeploy vllm/vllm-openai:v0.25.1 with the old args, verify /health, /v1/models, and one representative request, and re-run the benchmark. The response decides rollback first if the team cannot validate forward in the window, and never mutates the production deployment without a human directive naming target, scope, and rollback path.
assertions: Diagnosis uses exact image digests, serving args, model revision, nvidia-smi, and side-by-side startup logs
Investigates changed memory defaults or flag semantics together with the allocation phase rather than assuming the context limit directly sizes KV memory
The fix-forward path validates on a scratch instance with release notes and the frozen benchmark before redeploying
The rollback path redeploys the pinned previous image plus recorded config and verifies at the delivery boundary
No production mutation happens without a human directive naming target, scope, and rollback path

evals.prompt: Our old vLLM runbook says chunked prefill and prefix caching are off by default. We plan to add both flags and claim faster decoding because warm repeated system prompts reduce TTFT. Review this for V1/v0.26.0 and tell us what evidence is missing; do not change the server.
evals.expected_output: Correct the stale defaults with versioned/current official evidence: V1 enables chunked prefill where supported and v0.26.0 CacheConfig enables prefix caching. CacheConfig is not a universal resolved engine default: versioned EngineArgs leaves hybrid-model prefix caching opt-in and has backend exceptions. Inspect the installed engine/model/backend and resolved startup settings rather than assuming either flag changes behavior. Separate TTFT/prefill benefits from TPOT/decode work and propose matched cold/warm, shared/non-shared prefix measurements before a performance claim. No mutation is performed.
assertions: Explains that V1 chunked prefill is enabled where supported rather than generally off
Identifies the v0.26.0 CacheConfig prefix-caching default without treating it as a universal resolved engine setting
Requires inspection of the installed release and resolved startup settings before deciding whether enablement changes behavior
Distinguishes prefix-cache prefill or TTFT savings from direct new-token decoding acceleration
Proposes matched cold/warm and shared/non-shared prefix cohorts
Links official versioned or current vLLM documentation supporting the default correction

evals.prompt: A GGUF checkpoint is smaller than our native checkpoint. Can we treat it as an equally optimized drop-in replacement in vLLM and skip serving benchmarks? We are checking current docs but may deploy an older pinned engine.
evals.expected_output: Reject the drop-in/performance assumption. Cite the official GGUF warning that support is experimental, under-optimized and potentially feature-incompatible. Current documentation uses the out-of-tree vllm-gguf-plugin and recommends the base-model tokenizer, but older releases may differ. Pin/check engine/plugin/model compatibility and required API features, then compare quality and matched serving measurements. Do not install or deploy just to answer.
assertions: Describes vLLM GGUF support as experimental and under-optimized
Warns that GGUF may be incompatible with required serving features
Identifies the current out-of-tree vllm-gguf-plugin integration path
Checks the pinned engine version instead of applying the current plugin requirement universally to older releases
Recommends the matching base-model tokenizer
Requires measured serving evidence instead of inferring speed or parity from smaller file size
Requires task-quality validation before treating the GGUF checkpoint as an equivalent replacement

evals.prompt: We have ten active coding agents, but the benchmark stopped at four client requests. Startup printed a maximum concurrency of 20 at the configured context length; a colleague wants to set production to 18 and cite aggregate tokens/sec as completed work. Design the next vLLM test without running it.
evals.expected_output: Use configurable outstanding-request levels 1, 2, 4, 8, 10, extending if useful and safe, instead of four as a ceiling or 90% of the startup estimate. Declare numeric SLO/error/memory/thermal/budget stop constraints first and leave unsafe higher points untested. Separate active agents and tool waits from requested/client-in-flight, queued and running inference. Freeze actual context/output mix, model/engine/config, hardware, sampling and cache cohorts; repeat runs with per-request latency tails, preemption and memory evidence. Keep errors, timeouts, retries and finish reasons. Report accepted distinct tasks/hour only with a fixed task rubric and linked task-level evaluation; preserve failed/pending tasks and retry/tool-wait time in the measurement boundary.
assertions: Includes eight and ten in a configurable sweep rather than stopping at four
Allows extending the sweep beyond ten when safe and useful
Defines explicit stop constraints before escalating load
Rejects a fixed percentage of startup concurrency as proof of production SLO capacity
Separates active agents from requested, queued and running inference overlap
Requires per-request latency tails rather than relying solely on aggregate token throughput
Retains request errors in the benchmark outcome evidence
Retains timeouts in the benchmark outcome evidence
Records retry counts rather than treating every attempt as distinct completed work
Records finish reasons or truncation so shortened answers are not silently counted as equivalent work
Defines accepted tasks/hour using distinct tasks and linked task-acceptance evaluation
Keeps retry and tool-wait time inside the declared end-to-end task measurement boundary
Matches actual context/output distributions and cache cohorts across compared runs
Collects preemption and memory evidence during the sweep

evals.prompt: We changed max-model-len from 32768 to 16384. The measured requests still use 4096 prompt tokens plus 1024 generated tokens and the GPU memory budget did not change. Can we say we halved KV memory and doubled concurrency? Explain how to verify.
evals.expected_output: No automatic halving/doubling follows. max-model-len controls admission; the profiled/configured KV pool and actual resident token blocks are separate quantities. The unchanged real lengths do not imply lower per-request KV demand. Record pool bytes/tokens, occupancy and sharing, runtime overhead and startup assumptions, then run a matched SLO sweep. Check whether the new cap rejects or truncates other real tasks and report that rather than counting them as a speedup.
assertions: Distinguishes the request admission limit, allocated KV pool and actual resident token demand
Rejects automatic memory halving or concurrency doubling at unchanged actual token lengths
Requires memory profiling and a matched workload/SLO measurement before claiming improved capacity
Checks whether the lower limit rejects or truncates tasks rather than assuming quality is unchanged
